text: Good afternoon. My name is Lauren Chernoff, and I am calling this May 6th, 2026, Specialized Programs and Centers Committee meeting to order. I am joined tonight by my colleague, Mr. John Pepper, and Ms. Donahue is absent tonight. We are going to get started with item .2.01, which is public comment. We have one speaker tonight. I'll give you three minutes, and Mr. Paul Vickers, you may begin when you're ready.

Thank you, Ms. Chernoff. I thought I only had one minute, so I really practiced this and was going to be talking really fast. So I'm going to take a little relaxation break here and just start by saying I'm the principal of Hillsborough Charter Academy, Paul Vickers, and I had a very good conversation this morning with Justin Donovan from DDI. And I came to him with appreciation for our relationship with DDI over the

last decade, as long as we've been a charter school. And one of the things that I think, obviously, Mr. Pepper, you and Ms. Chernoff are aware, as a charter school, we pay $20,000 a year for our agreement with DDI, and it covers tech repair, some purchasing. But really honestly,

DDI has been very, very favorable to work with for many years, and I'm sure they will continue to be. And we're obviously very interested in maintaining our agreement with LCPS for the $20,000 that we spend. But we are a bit confused with some of the changes that are being proposed in the tech agreement as it pertains to our school and Middleburg Community Charter School as well.

The two schools have some similar needs and some differing needs. But we both do pay the $20,000. And one of the things that I was talking to Justin about is, within the proposed revisions of that tech agreement, it's not very specific. It doesn't really identify which pieces of technology

will continue to be serviced and which would not. And so we've asked Justin if we could please have an itemized list of that so that we can make better sense of it, truthfully. And furthermore, in the conversation that I had with Justin this morning, he was talking about the intercom system that was worked on over at Middleburg. And that concerned me because,

obviously, an intercom and some of the safety and security technology that is essential at every school should certainly be considered essential at our schools as well. Certainly all 144 of our scholars are LCPS students. Our teachers are all LCPS teachers. Obviously, I don't think anybody in the

school district, certainly not the school board, would want any of the children to be less safe than children at other schools. That's your time. Okay. Well, my three minutes were well used. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Vickers, for being here and advocating. And I will look forward to that discussion. All right. We will now move on to item number 3.01, approval of the draft minutes from our April 8th, 2026, meeting. Have you had a chance to review

them, Mr. Pepper? And do you have any edits or changes? I have had a chance to review them, Chair Chernoff, and I do not have any edits or changes. So with that, I will move that we approve the draft minutes from our April 8th, 2026, meeting. Do I have a second? I will second that. All in favor? Aye. Aye. That passes, so the minutes are approved. All right. Now, we will move into our topic about charter schools. So, we are on our first information item 4.01, Charter School

Annual Technical and Support Services Agreement. And Ms. Elaine Lehman, the Director of Elementary and Charter Schools, will kick us off and introduce the others that are joining us today. Thank you, Ms. Lehman. The floor is yours. Thank you, Mrs. Chernoff. We have two agreements. These are both annual renewals for those who haven't been with us before. Support services contract, you will see no changes to that contract. It's simply an annual renewal, and what changes each year in that contract are the rates,

the hourly rates, which come to us at some point during the summer months. So there have been no proposed changes to that agreement. It's just something that needs to be signed each year. But if you turn your attention to the tech support contract, you'll see that there are some redline changes. And for a description and explanation of those changes, I'm going to turn this over to Justin Donovan from the Department of Digital Innovation to explain those changes. Thank you very much.

So first, I thought I would start with a high-level overview of the intent behind these changes. As you know, these charter schools were formed a decade or so or more ago. And at the time when the charter schools were formed, the board at that time made a decision that it was just more financially responsible for the school district to stop operationally spending on these buildings and these schools, and that's when the charter schools were formed.

The charter community came in and said, "Hey, we would like to run a school here." Through those agreements and through that process, the technology equipment inside of those schools was purchased by the charter schools.And since then, they've been in a technology services contract with us where we support that equipment. We help them maintain it, and when it breaks, we help them resolve the challenges and get it back to working again.

As time has gone on, the technology in those buildings has grown in age, and we're starting to see areas in which this technology that was purchased by the charter schools is getting to a point to where it might not be possible to continue repairing it. We would need to do a full replacement. And the example I give in my conversation with Paul earlier was, for example, the PA system.

So in reviewing the contract for this year, we found that there was some ambiguity in the contract on whose responsibility it was financially to replace the equipment the charter schools purchased. So the intent behind these changes was simply to get rid of that ambiguity, make sure that everyone understood whose responsibility it was financially to replace those pieces of technology. Even though they have a services for repair contract with us,

we wanted to make that distinction between a replacement and a repair. So that's the intent and a little bit of the history on why those changes were made. The other changes you'll see in the agreement are related to name changes for where we've stopped using a piece of technology, and we've substituted it with the new piece of technology, the software. So with that being said, did you want me to stop and let you ask questions, or do we want to go line by line and go over each of the

red lines? I just have a quick question, if that's at all possible. And this is maybe more for my understanding of the finance and operations piece. This could be actually a question, I know we have some charter school principals here who might enlighten us a little bit. Where does the $20,000 they're spending come from? Is it a separate budget that they have? Per the agreement, it is, I think it's four equal payments of $5,000 that are transferred from the charter school to LCPS.

That is a Chair and Willoughby conversation probably. But that money is then paid for the services annually per this contract. So I believe all of that is spelled out in the contract- Okay ... the funding that's required. And so that has been $20,000 pretty much. When we first started, there was an a la carte contract where you could pick and choose what you wanted, and that became very cumbersome to manage the time and materials contract, so it became a single services contract. And just to level set what that $20,000 covers,

it covers internet connectivity, which is about $1,000 a month for resilient dark fiber connectivity and data center connectivity and our front-facing internet connectivity. So out of the gate, $12,000 of that $20,000 goes to internet connectivity. So it leaves about $8,000 to cover Xerox lease, phone services, other contractual maintenance services, plus technician time for when we have to send a technician to the school to do repairs. So that's what's included in that $20,000 contract.

So really, it's just a services contract, not a system equipment replacement refresh contract. And it's $20,000 regardless of whether or not they use $20,000 worth of services? Correct. Or they go over $20,000 worth of services. Correct. It's $20,000. I believe the first year, that's one of the reasons we had this ebb and flow, and it was-- So we just agreed on what we'd see typical break fix for a student device, how many times we would do that, and we built an average, and that's where the $20,000 came from. Okay.

Again, most of that goes toward just paying direct services for Xerox, phones, and internet connectivity. Can I back this out to a slightly higher level, if possible, just for my edification as someone relatively new on the board who's worked in the public sphere, not as much in the charter sphere. Where does that pool of money that then the charter schools are allocating the $20,000 come from? Is it a situation where we're giving them money and then they're giving it back?

I'm so glad you're here. All right. Good. I appreciate you guys being here. Yeah. Thank you. Yeah, so can I answer your question, and Paul can also chime in as well. So quarterly, like you said as well, that we get a per pupil allotment that we receive per scholar. And so from that, so we get a quarterly check that you take out staff benefits, staff salaries, and we get those quarterly. So from that $5,000 per quarter, that comes from the per pupil allotment. So it's just like a pool of money,

and you just take out money off of those things and so to answer your question, yeah, it's like- ... it's from the students we have at our school. Yeah. That's where it comes from. Okay. That's really appreciative. Yeah. So maybe this is more, I'm looking at this from the operations, because I also serve on finance and operations, looking at this from a finance and operations purview. And this is maybe a larger question for just us to think about and debate. Does this contract make sense?

So in doing some, just research about level setting spend per student, so in the FY 27 CIAN, the per pupil cost is $25,490, and there's a specific call-out where that's broken down, and it's about $903 per student that's dedicated to technology. So out of that, if you take the $20,000 and you divide it by the 144 scholars, we're at about $138 per student for technology. So services of what they're paying for versus what the complete,

what LCPS pays for. Now, my understanding is that that per pupil allotment is given to schools to make that decision about how they want to spend that. So LCPS is choosing $900 per student, and that covers everything from system repair, equipment, all of our refresh cycles for everything that we do across the division. And so there is a disparity there. But the $20,000 is really intended just to cover a services contract to provide, to keep existing things up and running. I appreciate that clarification.

That's a really good level set to frame this discussion. I really appreciate that. I don't know if you want to come along, Mr. Vickers. Oh, sure. Is that okay? Mr. Vickers has something to say. And thank you, Mr. Pepper. One thing that is important to know is that as a charter school, we do pay for our own computers, our own Promethean boards. And so when they're being refreshed, I think the computers are every

four years, and I believe Promethean boards are every seven years. That's our responsibility to pay for that. So, the $109 or whatever the number was, I can't quite remember, it doesn't necessarily include everything that the other schools would be receiving for their students. That's very helpful knowledge, and thank you for sharing that as well, Mr. Vickers. So I think we can move on, just sort of giving the highlights

of, I don't need to go through the entire thing, but just where the red line is, if we could just kind of summarize what that change specifically means, especially with the questions I know that we had from public comment and that I received from MCCS, too, about just the clarity about what's included and how does all that fall under here would be a good clarification. So, Mr. Donovan or Mr. Smith. Well, I think that there's a lot of just restructuring, so I don't think that there's any intention that anything's different.

It's just clarifying, removing some legacy terminology. So if you go to Technology Services 4, Section 2, it really is pulling out there's no obligation to refresh and replace computers, laptops, and that really is added as a specific item there. So it's not been buried under one item. So that is actually moved to 4A6, where it says there's no obligation to replace technology. So there's not any sort of intent to shift that.

It's just, again, realigning the language so it's easier to find and more clearly spelled out. The next change is really add-on services. We no longer use Blackboard, we use Aptigy, so just changing to whatever the modern tool is. The next is really just grouping computer, desktop, laptop, other to just technology equipment, as those shift and evolve. And then the last item is just highlighting that replacement of hardware, that

we are not obligated, and especially as we get into some of this equipment, keep in mind that when the charter schools took ownership of the facility, that equipment was already five or 10 years old, and it hasn't been replaced or refreshed. We would typically have a standard refresh process that would replace network equipment every seven years. So those type of refresh cycles we do for an existing facility aren't part of DDI's responsibility to do that for these.

So that's just why that language is there, is we are not budgeting because we are not allocated funding to do those typical refresh cycle replacements. I appreciate that. Mr. Pepper, did you have any other thoughts or questions? The only one I would have, Madam Chair, would be, I see that in 4A, the original what was

6 about AV devices and their connectivity, excluding Promethean boards, that section was redacted. Is there just reasoning behind the redaction of the connectivity of AV devices? That was a repeat of-- Where does it say that? I think 1. Is it in 1? Okay. Yeah, it's also in 1. So it was repetitive, so I removed that. Okay. Appreciate that. It just seemed weirdly out of place, but that's okay.

Yeah, I don't have anything on this as well. I am very appreciative of you walking us through this and the changes, and I've been on the board for a little bit now, so I'm feeling like I'm starting to sort of understand a lot of the way that things work. This really isn't DDI specific, so I'm kind of going to go off grid here a little bit. And I will work on this, and I will consult, and we

can work on if there's anything that needs to be changed or included. I thought these changes were more substantive than what you're saying, so I think that that is good. But I always, and I'm just going to be candid, I always sense tension here when talking about the charter schools, and I feel like we're having the same conversation over and over again with the same arguments over and over again. And maybe that's just me and my perception.

I'm new to special programs this year, so I wasn't sitting in on the conversations at the ground level with the charter schools, but I did get a lot of feedback at the full board, and I've been out to the charter schools, and I've seen the kids and been part of that. I talked to staff when we were looking at this to plan for the meeting, and it feels like everything is in these little bits and pieces, but we're having the same conversation. And so for me, what I would really like to do, kind

of to your point, is like, is this needed? I think it is. I think there's purpose here to these contracts and what we have with the charter schools, absolutely, in terms of that accountability and how that ebbs and flows, and we talk a lot about what the original vision was, and then we move into where we are now and that it feels like it's getting more difficult to sustain those things at this phase of where I'm at in this process with the school board. That's just how I feel about it. But what I would really like to see us move towards in the

future is a way to get sort of all of these things on the same timeline so that we're having a fulsome conversation across these different contracts and entities, whether that's the calendar or about being in the CIP or the tech-... technology agreement or facilities. I feel like that's why we're having these same sort of philosophical conversations that keep arising out of these little technical changes,

and I don't know that that's always necessary, and I think we could probably find a nice package deal that more fulsomely explores where we do stand with the charters. Because every time these little technical changes happen, we're all of a sudden opening this door of, "These are our kids. They're LCPS kids, they're LCPS schools." And I don't know that that's a super healthy thing for us to keep hashing out. I personally do see them as our LCPS kids.

I think there's some incredible programs happening at our schools. We're talking here all the time about new programs and new things to model after. We're going to see other schools that have other programs. So we have two right in our backyard that are doing amazing things. And so what I would like to see is just a consistent model through this committee that sort of tightens this up a little bit, really analyzes what is needed and what is not, and maybe reframe the conversation. We're way further down the road in terms of the age of these buildings, and the age of these devices, and the age of these schools.

They're also further down the road in what they've done with their curriculum, and their students, and their lottery process, and I would rather have that conversation all at once because it just keeps kicking up the dust on this. And honestly, if I had a kid there, it would be making me feel kind of bad, because we just keep going there. And so if we're going to go there, I guess we need to go there and have that tension conversation, but I would much rather us just get on the same page, get on a good cycle, and

move forward with where we're at with the charters. Because for me, I just hate to have to keep doing this tug-of-war, and I know that there is a lot that needs to be worked out. So that's my soapbox for tonight. You're welcome. But I really feel like it needed to be said. I think it sort of hit a head for me at this time because now I feel like I have had this conversation over the years so many times. So I appreciate you listening. I don't really have any questions, except that maybe is that possible for

us to try and align some of these things so that we can really get a more fulsome picture? So I would just say that the technology services contract is really a roll-up contract to the overall charter agreement contract, which is not a direct purview of DDI. So we're facilitating technology services based off of that master agreement. So whatever that master agreement, whatever the board decides to do, would drive what these contracts do and what would be included and not included. So, I think that this is just a

subset of that larger discussion, which we are more than happy to listen to, but really not in our purview about those kind of master agreements. No, I appreciate that context, and like I said, it wasn't really DDI-directed, it's just sort of an overall feeling that I've had. So I appreciate that, and that is good feedback for us as a board to really start there maybe and then work our way down. So I will hope to continue some of those conversations. Like I said, I will

do some thinking about this and some more understanding before we bring it back. But I think we can bring it back for action next time, so we'll plan to do that. All righty. Thank you guys so much for being here. I appreciate it. Thank you to the principals who are here. Appreciate your presence, as always, and we will move on to item 4.02, special programs update. And there are lots of friends joining us today, so I will pass it over to Ms. Katie Clark when
she gets settled, the director of academic programs, to introduce all the friends at the table. And we'll take a minute here to transition.

All right. Good afternoon, and thank you for the opportunity to share our special programs yearly overview. This will be part one. Today's update will highlight select special programs with additional programs and academies planned for the meeting in June. I'm joined this afternoon by several colleagues who will introduce themselves as they share updates on their respective programs. I would also like to acknowledge we have Jeff Adam in the audience, our principal at Heritage, which supports our IB program.

Thank you for being here. Without your leadership and support and all of our principals that house special programs, these programs would not be possible. So thank you for being here. Also want to thank Dr. Dave Blakelock from research for his support and his team's support with some of the data that you're going to see this afternoon. With that, here's our agenda. We're going to give a brief overview of special programs outreach efforts this year and the connection to the policy

and regulation 5115. Program-specific highlights today will include an overview, data, achievements, and identified opportunities for the following programs. We'll have dual language immersion, health and medical sciences, International Baccalaureate, the diploma program, and lastly, the Naval Junior Reserve Officers Training Corps. We will provide a little bit of time in between each program, we'll keep an eye on

time, to share any feedback for you guys to ask any questions. So after each program, we'll pause, so that you guys can ask questions you have. This year, our special programs outreach focused on increasing awareness, access, and community engagement. We hosted two special program fairs in September at Heritage High School and Parkview High School. Those featured a student panel representing all special programs, and it had breakout sessions for families to attend.

We also held eighth-grade assemblies countywide to ensureAll students received direct information about program options, and we followed up with a countywide individual school email to both families and students regarding important program information. We developed special program videos that are linked in School Links, and those are really to start advertising even as young as elementary school families and students can see those videos through School Links.

We also published the first edition of the Special Programs magazine, and each program held their individual program information nights at their schools, along with presenting at committees such as LEAF, GEAC, and SEAC, along with others. We collaborated with principals, counselors, and parent liaisons to ensure consistent messaging across all of our schools. We did conduct a follow-up special programs and academy survey per the Special Programs Committee

advice last fall, providing valuable feedback to guide future programming. So currently, we are planning the expansion of dual language immersion at Leesburg Elementary starting this fall. We are preparing for the launch of the Academy of Global and Linguistic Studies this fall, and we are in the application phase for the IB Career Program and the expansion of ROTC to include Army. Over the past several years, LCPS has significantly expanded its special

programs and opportunities, and we just want to say thank you to our school board for its continued support in making these opportunities possible for our students. LCPS Policy and Regulation 5115 requires that the school board receive regular updates on each of our established special programs yearly. With that framework in mind, I will now turn it over to Kelly James, Supervisor of World Languages and Cultures, who will provide an overview of the Dual Language Immersion program.

Thank you. So just to provide a brief program overview, we currently have dual language immersion at two schools, Potomac Elementary and Sanders Corner Elementary, expanding to Leesburg next year. Our model is a 50/50, two-way, two-teacher immersion program that begins in kindergarten and is projected to progress through fifth grade. Students spend half their day learning in Spanish and the other half learning in English.

Students are selected through a lottery selection, and transportation is not provided for students living outside of the attendance area. This is our current enrollment that shows our dual language immersion program is operating at or near full capacity across all sites, demonstrating a strong and sustained program. This chart is our DLI cohort retention.

So this is students who were enrolled in DLI at either school in September 30th of each year. We currently have the past two cohorts. We will have the 2025 cohort information after this year. The '23-'24 cohort of students are now in second grade, and they're shown in the first graph labeled the 2023 cohort. You can see that our retention for Potomac is 83%, and Sanders is 96%.

And for the '24-'25 cohort of students that are currently in first grade, we have a retention of 87% at Potomac and 94%. It's important to note that this is students who started in the program and are currently still there. That doesn't mean that we have open seats at the program, as I just showed, but because we're able to fill those seats in kindergarten and first grade and second. This is demonstrating the Spanish

proficiency progress in all four are in listening and in speaking, with our cohorts in the fall and in the spring. We're still in the process of finalizing our spring data. But we collect, since they are still creating the skills for reading and writing, we are primarily assessing listening and speaking.

And this does show growth from the fall to the spring in each year. This is our VALS reading risk data for kindergarten at both of our schools. That's comparing both our DLI students and our non-dual language immersion students. The kindergarten VALS data shows a strong overall shift from students who are identified from mid and high risk readings categories

into the low-risk performance by spring. Across both of our schools, some students are demonstrating meaningful early literacy growth with significant increases in the percentage of students identified as low risk. So it's on par with their non-DLI peers. For our students who are in first grade, we see strong literacy development across both schools. Potomac especially shows significant movement of students from mid risk into low risk. Sanders maintains a high proportion of students

in the low-risk category with stable performance over time. And for our students who are currently in second grade, we did see a slight increase in high-risk levels from fall to winter for second-grade students at Potomac. But we saw a significant decrease of students from the mid-risk level to low risk following the DLI trend at Potomac. And we are still in the process of assessing students for the spring data, so we don't have that data to share quite yet.

But this is just from fall to winter. Our dual language immersion program continues to show strong results in the three key areas of student success, family engagement, and program growth. Students are making steady progress in both Spanish and English, meeting academic expectations. Families are highly engaged through parent institutes, cultural celebrations, community information sessions, and school-based events that strengthen that home and school connection.We've also expanded

successfully across multiple schools and grade levels, maintaining strong outcomes and alignment with state guidance. Some of our highlights include our Summer Science Fiesta, Hispanic Heritage Month events, international events, bilingual presentations, and increased access through countywide information sessions. We've also identified some opportunities for ways that we can continue to improve our program, and those are navigating concerns with the amount of time spent on assessing on the English side.

So that's something that we're looking at ways that we can improve and support our schools in that way. We also have identified some opportunities and concerns with hiring for teachers on both sides, especially for Spanish, as well as finding ways that we can expand the support of our language ambassador across both classrooms. And those are things that we're looking into ways that we can... Those are opportunities for us to better support our schools.

And we are happy to hear any questions or feedback that you might have. Mr. Pepper? Certainly. Thank you, Madam Chair. Couple questions for you, not anything, just more curiosity. How does the dual language proficiency of students, because I know there's a little bit of a cohort dropout. It's not significant. It's really small, actually. It's pretty impressive that it's that small. But a student who joins the DLI program, perhaps in first or second

grade, how do their language proficiency, speaking and writing, compare to those of the students who have been in since kindergarten? We just don't have the data yet because it's so new. So if a student is not a heritage Spanish speaker, and if there's a seat that opens because somebody has moved, again, the seats that are open are primarily because students are moving out of the county. Mm-hmm. They are able to because they don't have that foundational knowledge.

Once they are in second grade, there is those two years of language proficiency that's there, so they do need to have some Spanish-speaking background once they're in second grade. So we do have a way to assess students to make sure that they have the prerequisite language foundation to support learning content in the language. When we have had students who have come in in first grade, who miss that first year of kindergarten,

we have not seen too much of a lag. They're able to pick that up pretty quickly. But again, we only have that one year of data then if they're students who are in second grade, and they just joined last year, so we only have that one year. Okay. That's- But they're performing on par with the other dual language immersion students. It's really good to know that they just don't come in and they're suddenly in a world where they don't speak the language that they're being instructed in, so that's important. You mentioned challenges in staffing and hiring, and just looking at the numbers,

I'm assuming it's two classrooms at each school that are dual language. So, what's the process for finding both a teacher who's certified in elementary education and a teacher who is a native speaker of these-- I'm assuming they're native speakers of these languages for the most, primarily, yeah. They are. Yeah. What's that looking like, and where do you see

opportunities to find people who can meet these qualifications? And is there some incentive we can offer to find these really niche individuals? Yes. So previously, it was like looking for a unicorn, finding somebody who had the level. It's not a requirement that they're a native speaker, but there is a level of proficiency that they have to have. So native-like. And previously, they had to have both of those things, which was very hard to find. So we have worked with HRTD. There's a third-party

group that we've worked with for finding those individuals. But we've also received guidance from the state, where there are other ways to get teachers who have either one endorsement or the other to have the actual dual language immersion endorsement from the state. So then they would be qualified. There's a course or there's an assessment that they take, both of those, that is provided that they just have to sign up and take, and then they are certified to teach DLI.

Have we thought- Go ahead. Have we thought about offering some sort of additional stipend, or do we, for teachers who participate in this program? It seems pretty unique and somewhat of an additional responsibility. Just going to put that out there as a thought. Thank you. I will piggyback a little bit off of that in terms of staffing. I actually, after seeing it, which thank you very much for

organizing very fulsome visits. I got to be in every class. And the one we didn't get to see because the teacher was at PD, I actually went back another time to see her because I heard she was so amazing, and I had to. So, seeing it totally changed my perspective of it, and it's no fault to you with the presentations. I think presentations are great, but I think it speaks to that ability to when you actually get in the building, and you talk to the teachers, and you see the kids, especially the engagement piece.

You can type on a slide, like, "Kids are-- We're seeing that they're engaged." But when you're there, and they're like... It was amazing. And there's a lot of them because the class sizes are a little bit bigger. So the fact that they are managed that way and the excitement in the room, and I think actually, the staffing, the extra workload is actually falling on the English side, if I'm not mistaken, with the testing that they have to do for both groups and, I think,

just some additional things that they have. So that would actually be the piece that I would look at in terms of increasing for a stipend because they are also having larger class sizes along colleagues who have smaller class sizes who don't have the dual language component, which is another thing I didn't realize until we saw that. So I think that that could be a consideration, but for me, that was sort of an aha. It was like, oh, the English side is doing the heavy lifting.

So we always appreciate visiting schools with you, Ms. Chernov. But also having a chance to talk to that principal, that is something staff's having conversations about in terms of supporting the English teacher side of the coin. So we can definitely look at stipends and see what makes sense. We've also talked about finding other ways for testing support, whether that's through part-time funds, people that could push in and help with the lift, looking at the balance between the two teachers.

So this is some definitely feedback we received from that visit and what we've been hearing from schools. We need to balance staying true to our model. It is still a new program, but we also need to be responsive to the feedback of principals, in particular our teachers, in terms of the experience they're having. So the team is definitely open to ideas, and we appreciate the feedback you're giving us. Yeah, and I love that we can see the student retention. I think that's important, but I think the teacher retention is also equally

important and sort of understanding why they may stay in or roll out. So that'll be something that I would love to continue to look at. And I really appreciate what you just said, Mr. Slevin, about being responsive to the principals, because when we were there, there was a sort of sense of, "Well, we have to follow the rules.
